children.title: Inertia & the First Law
Why did Aristotle think motion needs a push?
children.summary: Pushes a toy car on carpet, wood and ice, and sees friction is the hidden force

children.title: Galileo's double incline: why would the ball roll forever?
children.summary: Flattens the second slope; the ball rolls farther to regain its height, and on a level slope it never stops (spec below)
children.spec: Setup: a ball released on the left slope rises to the same height on the right (no friction). Flatten: lowering the right slope makes the ball travel further to reach that height. Limit: at 0° the height is never reached, so the motion never stops: inertia. Reality: a friction slider shows why real balls stop.

children.title: Why are you thrown back when the bus starts?
children.summary: Sees your feet go with the floor while your body stays put

children.title: Why is 'W = R, so the book is at rest' backwards?
children.summary: Reasons from the observation: the book is at rest, so the forces must balance

children.title: Vega: inertia in ancient Indian thought
children.summary: Reads how the Vaiśeṣika idea of vega (persistent straight-line motion) anticipates inertia

children.title: An astronaut steps off an accelerating ship
children.summary: Loses all acceleration the instant they leave

children.title: Second Law & Momentum
Why momentum, not just velocity?
children.summary: Stops a car and a truck at the same speed, then a slow and a fast bullet

children.title: Why does a cricketer pull the hands back?
children.summary: Spreads the same Δp over a longer time and sees the force peak drop on the F–t graph

children.title: Why does the second law act here and now?
children.summary: Drops a stone from an accelerating train: no horizontal acceleration afterwards

children.title: Why does a force only change the velocity along it?
children.summary: Pushes sideways on a moving puck and watches the original component stay the same

children.title: Why isn't 'ma' another force?
children.summary: Labels every force as 'force on A by B'; ma is the effect, not a cause

children.title: F = ma and impulse solver
children.summary: Solves force problems and computes impulse (a 12 m/s ball hit straight back = 3.6 N s)

children.title: A bullet into a wooden block
children.summary: Stops a bullet in 60 cm, needing an average force of 270 N

children.title: Weighing scale in a lift
children.summary: Rides up, down and in free fall and watches the reading change

children.title: Third Law & Momentum Conservation
Why don't action and reaction cancel?
children.summary: Draws each force on its own body

children.title: Why does a falling stone pull Earth up just as hard?
children.summary: Compares equal forces with very different accelerations

children.title: Why is momentum conserved?
children.summary: Pairs the third law with the second over a shared time interval

children.title: How does a horse pull a cart at all?
children.summary: Draws the free-body diagrams; the ground's push decides

children.title: Find the action–reaction pairs
children.summary: Matches the force pairs in a scene

children.title: Gun recoil
children.summary: Fires a 20 g shell at 80 m/s from a 100 kg gun: recoil 1.6 cm/s

children.title: Ball off a wall at an angle
children.summary: Sees the force on the wall is always normal to it

children.title: Equilibrium & Free-Body Diagrams
Why do three forces in equilibrium close a triangle?
children.summary: Lays the force arrows tip to tail and they return to the start

children.title: Why does a free-body diagram show only forces ON the body?
children.summary: Chooses the system and filters out everything else

children.title: Free-body diagram builder
children.summary: Drags forces onto the chosen body

children.title: Resolve and solve
children.summary: Pulls a rope sideways with 50 N under a 60 N load and solves the angle along two axes

children.title: Block, pulley and trolley
children.summary: Finds a = 0.96 m/s² and T = 27.1 N

children.title: Friction
Why is static friction self-adjusting?
children.summary: Pushes harder and harder; friction matches the push until it reaches μₛN

children.title: Why doesn't friction depend on contact area?
children.summary: Turns a brick on its side; the force is the same (an empirical law, not a fundamental one)

children.title: Why is friction what moves cars and walkers forward?
children.summary: Puts a car on ice and watches the wheels spin with nowhere to push

children.title: Why does the slip angle give μₛ = tan θ?
children.summary: Tilts a plane until the block slides; mass cancels

children.title: Why is rolling friction so much smaller?
children.summary: Compares sliding, rolling and ball bearings

children.title: Why are contact forces electrical at heart?
children.summary: Zooms into a surface to see electron clouds pushing back

children.title: Incline calculator
children.summary: Finds the forces and acceleration on a rough slope

children.title: A box in an accelerating train
children.summary: Stays put up to a = μₛg = 1.5 m/s²

children.title: Circular Dynamics
Why isn't centripetal force a new force?
children.summary: Finds the real force in each case: tension, friction or gravity

children.title: Why do you feel pushed outward on a merry-go-round?
children.summary: Separates the real inward force from the feeling of impending motion

children.title: Why does a level turn have a speed limit?
children.summary: Raises the speed until friction can't supply mv²/R: v_max = √(μₛRg)

children.title: Why does banking help?
children.summary: Tilts the road so the normal force leans inward: v₀ = √(Rg tan θ) needs no friction

children.title: Why does a stone fly off along the tangent?
children.summary: Cuts the string mid-swing

children.title: Will the cyclist slip?
children.summary: Takes a 3 m turn at 18 km/h with μ = 0.1: yes

children.title: A banked race track
children.summary: Uses a 300 m radius banked at 15°: optimum speed 28.1 m/s

children.title: Work & Kinetic Energy
Why does only the force along the motion do work?
children.summary: Pulls a box at an angle; W = F·d = Fd cos θ

children.title: Why does pushing a wall do no work but tire you?
children.summary: Sees zero displacement means zero work, while muscles still use internal energy

children.title: Why is the work–energy theorem v² = u² + 2as in disguise?
children.summary: Multiplies the kinematic equation by m/2

children.title: Why is variable-force work the area under F–x?
children.summary: Slices the F–x curve into rectangles (spec below)
children.spec: Curve: drag points to shape F(x). Slices: n rectangles F(xᵢ)Δx, summed live. Limit: as n grows the sum converges to the area, ∫F dx. Check: a spring F = kx gives the triangle ½kx².

children.title: Why don't third-law pairs do equal and opposite work?
children.summary: Skids a cycle: the road does −2000 J on it, the cycle does 0 on the road

children.title: Dot-product work calculator
children.summary: Finds the angle and work from components

children.title: A raindrop's energy budget
children.summary: Sees gravity does 10 J while air takes away 8.75 J

children.title: A bullet through plywood
children.summary: Keeps 10% of its KE but 32% of its speed

children.title: Potential Energy & Conservation
Why do only some forces have a potential energy?
children.summary: Walks gravity and friction around a closed loop: gravity's work is 0, friction's isn't (spec below)
children.spec: Loop: move a block around a closed path on a hill, with and without friction. Ledger: gravity's work around the loop sums to 0, friction's is negative. Path test: two different routes between the same points do equal gravity work but different friction work. Definition: only path-independent forces get V(x) with F = −dV/dx.

children.title: Why is F = −dV/dx?
children.summary: Rolls a ball on an energy landscape: it is pushed downhill, and harder where the slope is steep

children.title: Why is the zero of potential energy arbitrary?
children.summary: Moves the zero and sees every difference stay the same

children.title: Why is a spring's PE ½kx²?
children.summary: Reads the triangle under F = kx

children.title: Why is the speed at the bottom of any smooth slope √(2gh)?
children.summary: Changes the slope's shape: the speed only cares about the drop

children.title: Read an energy diagram
children.summary: Draws E across V(x) to find the turning points and forbidden regions

children.title: Energy bar chart
children.summary: Tracks K, V and E as bars through a motion

children.title: Loop-the-loop
children.summary: Needs v₀ = √(5gL) at the bottom to stay on the string at the top

children.title: Crash-test spring
children.summary: Compresses 2.00 m without friction, 1.35 m with friction

children.title: Power
Why is P = F · v?
children.summary: Divides dW = F·dx by dt

children.title: Why is a kWh energy, not power?
children.summary: Runs a 100 W bulb for 10 h: 1 kWh = 3.6 MJ

children.title: Lift motor power
children.summary: Lifts at 2 m/s against 22 kN: 44 kW, about 59 hp

children.title: Wind power grows as v³
children.summary: Doubles the wind speed and gets 8 × the power

children.title: Rooftop solar for a home
children.summary: Sizes the panel area for 8 kW at 200 W/m² and 20% efficiency

children.title: Collisions
Why is momentum always conserved but KE only sometimes?
children.summary: Compares elastic, inelastic and sticky collisions on one track

children.title: Why do equal masses swap velocities head-on?
children.summary: Plays Newton's cradle and solves the two conservation laws

children.title: Why does a ball bounce off a truck while the truck barely notices?
children.summary: Lets m₂ ≫ m₁ in the formulas

children.title: Why do equal-mass glancing collisions split at 90°?
children.summary: Pots a ball at 37° on a billiard table and finds the cue goes off at 53°

children.title: Why isn't KE conserved during the impact itself?
children.summary: Slows the collision down to show the spring-like squash

children.title: Collision lab
children.summary: Slides the coefficient of restitution from elastic to perfectly inelastic

children.title: Why does a reactor use heavy water or graphite?
children.summary: Slows neutrons: deuterium takes 8/9 of the KE per hit, carbon only 28%
